# Templates: Model Specs, Experiment Readouts, and Playbooks {#sec-templates}

This appendix collects the documents the book recommends writing, as templates that can be copied into a repository or a wiki. Each one is short on purpose. A template that takes an hour to fill in gets skipped, and one that takes ten minutes gets used. Delete sections that don't apply rather than writing "N/A", and link to dashboards, queries, and code rather than pasting them.

The templates are written in Markdown so they can live next to the code they describe. The same files are in the book's repository under `templates/`.

<!-- TODO: add the templates/ folder to the repo once the code pass starts. -->

## Model Spec

A model spec describes everything that changes a model's behavior, as in @sec-pipelines-validation-and-publishing, and everything the bidder needs to serve it, as in @sec-where-trees-stop. It's reviewed by the ML team and the bidder team before the first training run, and kept up to date as the model changes.

```markdown
# Model spec: <model name>

Owner: <team or pod>        Status: draft | review | serving | retired
Registry name: <name>       Spec version: <n>

## Purpose
- What the model predicts, for which campaigns or goals.
- Where the prediction enters the pricing ledger (A, κ, W(b), ...).
- What it replaces, if anything, and what it falls back to.

## Target and labels
- Label definition, with the attribution window and source table.
- Training window, label maturity cutoff, and how delayed labels are
  handled.
- Sampling: negative downsampling rate and the correction applied.

## Inputs
| Feature | Source (field or lookup) | Version | Default if missing |
|---|---|---|---|

## Transforms
- Reference to the preprocessing spec in the model bundle.
- Fitted artifacts (vocabularies, bucket boundaries) and where they're
  stored.

## Architecture and hyperparameters
- Model type, key hyperparameters, and the seed.
- Rendered training query hash: <hash>

## Evaluation
- Offline metrics: log loss, normalized entropy, AUC, calibration by
  segment.
- Slices that must not regress: <placements, geos, exchanges, top
  campaigns>.
- Validation gates that block publishing, with thresholds.

## Serving contract
- Input and output tensors, with types and shapes.
- Budgets: p99 latency, memory, CPU per request, and how they're
  measured.
- Golden vectors: location and tolerance.

## Fallbacks
- Behavior when the model fails to load, times out, or returns out-of-
  range values.
- The next level on the fallback ladder.

## Rollout
- Shadow plan, canary stages, and A/B test design (link to the
  experiment brief).
- Guardrails and automated rollback conditions.

## Monitoring
- Alerts on prediction distribution, calibration, missing inputs, and
  parity.
- Dashboard links and the playbook for each alert.
```

## Experiment Brief

Write the brief before an A/B test starts, as in @sec-shadow-mode-canaries-and-ab-tests. Most of the value is in deciding the primary metric, the guardrails, and the duration before seeing any results.

```markdown
# Experiment brief: <name>

Owner: <name>
Layer: <models | pricing | pacing | selection | creative>
Start: <date>      Planned end: <date>      Salt: <experiment salt>

## Hypothesis
- What we expect to change, and why, in one or two sentences.

## Design
- Arms and traffic shares.
- Randomization unit (device) and any exclusions.
- Budget split: how each campaign's budget is divided between arms.
- Other experiments running in the same layer, and why they don't
  conflict.

## Metrics
- Primary metric, with its label window and the day it becomes
  complete.
- Guardrails: spend, win rate, CPI or ROAS by top campaign, latency,
  fallback share.
- Minimum detectable effect and the duration that gives enough power.

## Stopping rules
- Conditions for stopping early: a failed guardrail, a broken test,
  clear losses.
- We won't stop early because it looks like a win.
```

## Experiment Readout

The readout turns the result into a decision, using the go/no-go checklist from @sec-shadow-mode-canaries-and-ab-tests. It's written for someone who didn't follow the test, so it leads with the decision.

```markdown
# Experiment readout: <name>

Decision: ship | don't ship | rerun | extend
Brief: <link>        Dates: <start> to <end>, complete days only

## Summary
- Two or three sentences: what changed, the primary result, and the
  decision.

## Validity
- [ ] No sample ratio mismatch (p-value: <p>)
- [ ] Each arm spent its share of budget
- [ ] No other changes landed in this layer during the test
- [ ] Labels complete for the reported window

## Results
| Metric | Control | Treatment | Change | 95% interval |
|---|---|---|---|---|

- Variance reduction used, if any.
- Segments examined, with a correction for the number of comparisons.

## Guardrails
- Any guardrail or major segment that got worse, and by how much.

## Does it make sense?
- How the result compares with the offline evaluation and the shadow
  comparison.
- Anything surprising, and what we checked to explain it.

## Next steps
- Rollout plan if shipping, or what we'd change for a rerun.
```

## Go/No-Go Checklist

For launches that aren't A/B tests, such as a new exchange, a new geo, or a new campaign type, the same questions apply in a lighter form.

```markdown
# Go/no-go: <launch>

- [ ] Shadow or listen-only run completed; predictions match offline
      within tolerance.
- [ ] Parity checks and golden vectors pass in the target environment.
- [ ] Kill switch tested for this launch's scope.
- [ ] Spend caps and bid caps configured.
- [ ] Alerts and dashboards in place; the on-call engineer knows it's
      launching.
- [ ] Rollback plan written and tested.
- [ ] Launch during working hours, with an owner watching the first
      hour.
```

## Playbook

A playbook is linked from each paging alert, as in @sec-operating-a-competitive-dsp. It answers the five questions the on-call engineer has when the alert fires.

```markdown
# Playbook: <alert name>

Alert: <link to definition>     Tier: 1 | 2     Owner: <team>

## What it means
- What the alert measures and what usually causes it.

## Confirm
- Dashboard panels to check, with links.
- Queries that split the signal by model version, host, exchange, or
  segment.

## Safe first actions
1. <for example, roll back the last deploy>
2. <for example, switch the model to its fallback>
3. <for tier 1: the kill switch for the affected scope>

## Escalate
- When: <conditions>
- To whom: <team and rotation>

## Verify recovery
- Which signals return to which band, and for how long.
```

## Postmortem

Every tier 1 incident, and any tier 2 incident with real impact, gets a blameless postmortem, as in @sec-operating-at-scale. The most important section is the last one: the guardrail that keeps the same class of incident from happening again.

```markdown
# Postmortem: <incident title>

Date: <date>     Tier: <tier>     Author: <name>
Status: draft | reviewed

## Summary
- What was the issue? Two or three sentences.

## Impact
- Duration, affected campaigns, exchanges, or geos.
- Spend at risk, overspend, and lost delivery.

## Timeline
| Time | Event |
|---|---|

## Detection
- How was it found? The alert, report, or person, and how long it
  took.

## Response
- How was it fixed? Actions taken, in order, and which ones helped.

## Root cause and contributing factors
- The cause, and the conditions that let it reach production.

## What we learned
- What went well, what didn't, and where we got lucky.

## Guardrails
| Action | Type (alert, fallback, check, test, gate) | Owner | Due |
|---|---|---|---|
```

## Decision Record

A decision record captures one decision, as in @sec-building-the-ml-team. Once accepted, it doesn't change. A later decision that revisits it is a new record that supersedes it.

```markdown
# Decision <number>: <title>

Date: <date>     Status: proposed | accepted | superseded by <number>
Deciders: <names>

## Context
- The problem, the constraints, and what forced a decision now.

## Decision
- What we chose, in one or two sentences.

## Options considered
| Option | Why not |
|---|---|

## Consequences
- What gets easier, what gets harder, and what we'll watch for.
- What would make us revisit this.
```

A record for something tried and paused is worth writing too, such as a deep model that a boosted model beat. The context and the numbers are what keep the team from rerunning the same experiment a year later without knowing why it stopped.
